title: Mata Sahib Kaur, mother of the Khalsa
hook: at amrit, Sikhs are told Mata Sahib Kaur is their spiritual mother

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Sundari, sending letters of counsel out of Delhi to a scattered people. Your line was she led. Did you write to anyone? A new week starts today, with a mother. Day eight hundred twenty.

Who are your parents? On most days that's a simple question with a simple answer. But at a Sikh amrit ceremony, once the new initiates have taken the amrit, they are given a new answer, a second family on top of the one they were born into. They are told who their spiritual father is, and who their spiritual mother is, and where their spiritual home is. People come to that moment from every kind of family. Some have lost a mother. Some never knew one. Some have a wonderful one. And all of them, standing together, are handed the same name. Today: Mata Sahib Kaur.
screen: `WHO ARE YOUR PARENTS?` → `A SECOND FAMILY AT AMRIT.` → `ONE MOTHER FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Mata Sahib Kaur was a wife of Guru Gobind Singh. Tradition says she had no children of her own, and that the Guru told her she would be the mother of a much larger family: the Khalsa. And that is how Sikhs remember her. At amrit, the new members of the Khalsa are told: your father is Guru Gobind Singh, your mother is Mata Sahib Kaur, and your home is Anandpur. Think about what that does. A shopkeeper's son and a farmer's daughter, people whose families might never have shared a meal, walk out of the ceremony as brothers and sisters, with the same mother. The family is not made by blood. It's made by the bowl. Two days ago, with Mata Jito, we heard that some tellings say it was Mata Sahib Kaur who added the sweets to the first amrit. Either way, the tellings put a woman's hand in that first bowl. After the Guru's death she lived in Delhi beside Mata Sundari, and tradition says she, too, sent letters of guidance to the sangats. Here is the quiet surprise in her story. A woman with no children of her own is remembered as mother to every member of the Khalsa. Being a mother, in this telling, is not only about giving birth. It's about who you hold, who you claim, who you treat as yours. And every time a new Sikh takes amrit, her name is said again.
screen: `A WIFE OF GURU GOBIND SINGH.` · `NO CHILDREN OF HER OWN.` · `YOUR MOTHER IS MATA SAHIB KAUR.` · `A FAMILY MADE BY THE BOWL.` · then, large: `MOTHER OF THE KHALSA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a spiritual mother. Let the breath settle. Think of a woman who cared for you in a way she didn't have to. Not necessarily your mother. A grandmother, an aunt, a teacher, a neighbor, a friend's mom whose kitchen was always open. Someone who claimed you as hers. Hold her in mind for a few breaths and remember one specific thing she did. If she's living, you might tell her later. If she's gone, just say her name quietly and say thank you. The bell holds the time.
Mata Sahib Kaur. A wife of Guru Gobind Singh, named at every amrit as the spiritual mother of the Khalsa. Today's word.
Your line: mother of the khalsa. Today, thank one woman who mothered you without having to, in person, by message, or in your own heart. Day eight hundred twenty.
